chapter.title: Delivery pipelines, infrastructure as code and the cloud
chapter.summary: Shipping changes automatically, describing infrastructure in code, and the core cloud building blocks.

lessons.title: CI/CD: pipelines, testing stages, deployments and supply-chain safety
lessons.summary: What continuous integration, delivery and deployment mean, how to design fast reliable pipelines, release strategies, GitOps, secrets in CI and securing the software supply chain.

parts.label: Continuous integration
parts.body:
## The point of CI/CD

The longer code sits unmerged, the more painful and risky integrating it becomes. **Continuous integration (CI)** means every change is merged into the main branch frequently (at least daily) and automatically built and tested. **Continuous delivery** means the main branch is always in a releasable state and can be deployed with one click. **Continuous deployment** goes further: every change that passes the pipeline is deployed to production automatically. The research behind DORA metrics shows teams that do this ship faster **and** more reliably.

The four **DORA metrics** to track: **deployment frequency**, **lead time for changes**, **change failure rate** and **time to restore service**.

## Anatomy of a pipeline

```
push / pull request
   │
   ▼
[ lint + typecheck ]──[ unit tests ]──[ build artifact ]──[ integration tests ]──[ security scans ]
                                              │
                                              ▼
                          publish immutable artifact (image tagged with commit SHA)
                                              │
                         deploy to staging ──► smoke / e2e tests ──► (approval?) ──► production
                                                                                      │
                                                                         verify, monitor, auto-rollback
```

Design principles:

1. **Fast feedback**: target under ~10 minutes for the PR check. Run cheap checks first (lint, types, unit), fail fast, parallelise independent jobs, cache dependencies and build layers, run only affected tests in monorepos.
2. **Build once, deploy many**: build an immutable artifact (container image) a single time, tagged by commit SHA, and promote **the same artifact** through environments. Never rebuild per environment: what you tested must be what you ship.
3. **Reproducible**: pinned dependencies and base images, containerised build environments, no reliance on the runner's state.
4. **Trustworthy**: flaky tests are bugs. Quarantine and fix them, because a pipeline people re-run until green stops meaning anything.
5. **Everything as code**: pipeline definitions (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkinsfile, CircleCI) live in the repo and are reviewed like code.
6. **Protected main**: required reviews, required status checks, no direct pushes.
7. **Configuration separate from the artifact**: environment-specific values are injected at deploy time (see twelve-factor).

## Test stages and what each buys

| stage | scope | speed | runs on |
|---|---|---|---|
| lint, format, type check | static | seconds | every commit |
| unit tests | pure logic | seconds | every commit |
| integration tests | real DB/queue in containers | minutes | every PR |
| contract tests | service boundaries | fast | every PR |
| end-to-end | deployed system, few critical journeys | slow | after deploy to staging, nightly |
| security: SAST, dependency audit, secret scan, image scan | code and artifacts | minutes | every PR |
| performance / load | latency and throughput budgets | slow | nightly or pre-release |

## Secrets and permissions in CI

- Never store secrets in the repo. Use the CI system's secret store, scoped per environment, and prefer **OIDC federation** (the CI job gets a short-lived cloud token by proving its identity) over long-lived cloud keys.
- Give each job the **least privilege**: read-only token by default, write only where needed.
- Don't expose secrets to pull requests from forks. Treat third-party actions/plugins as code you execute: pin them to a commit SHA.
- Mask secrets in logs; rotate regularly.

parts.label: Deployment and supply chain
parts.body:
## Release strategies

| strategy | how | pros | cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rolling** | replace instances gradually | no extra capacity; default in Kubernetes | two versions live at once; slow rollback |
| **Blue-green** | stand up a full new environment, switch traffic, keep old for rollback | instant switch and rollback | double capacity; database must work with both |
| **Canary** | send 1 to 5 percent of traffic to the new version, watch error rate and latency, then widen | tiny blast radius, real-traffic validation | needs good metrics and traffic routing |
| **Feature flags** | deploy code dark, enable per user or percent at runtime | decouples deploy from release; instant kill switch | flag debt; test both paths |
| **Shadow / dark launch** | mirror traffic to the new version without returning its responses | validates under real load | extra cost; avoid side effects |

**Automated rollback**: define health signals (error rate, latency, SLO burn) and roll back automatically when they breach during a canary (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker). **Database migrations** must be backward compatible (expand, migrate, contract) because old and new versions overlap.

## GitOps

Instead of CI pushing changes into a cluster, the **desired state lives in Git** and an agent in the cluster (Argo CD, Flux) pulls and applies it, continuously correcting drift. Benefits: every change is a reviewed commit, an audit trail for free, rollback is a `git revert`, and cluster credentials never leave the cluster. CI builds and pushes the image, then updates the image tag in the config repo.

## Software supply chain security

Most modern breaches arrive via dependencies and build systems, not your own code.

- **Pin and verify** dependencies: lockfiles, `npm ci`, hash-checked installs; review dependency updates (Dependabot/Renovate) and run `audit`.
- **SBOM** (software bill of materials) for each artifact to know what's inside; scan images (Trivy, Grype) and fail on critical issues.
- **Sign artifacts and verify at deploy** (Sigstore cosign); generate **provenance attestations** (SLSA levels) proving which source and builder produced an image.
- **Harden CI**: ephemeral runners, least-privilege tokens, pinned actions, protected branches and environments with required approvals, no `pull_request_target` footguns.
- **Secret scanning** on every push, and rotate anything exposed.
- Keep build and deploy permissions separate from developer laptops.

## Monorepos and speed

Use change detection (`paths` filters, Nx/Turborepo/Bazel affected graphs), remote caching, test sharding and parallel matrices. Large test suites: run fast tests on PRs and slower suites on merge or nightly, but never skip them entirely.

## Common anti-patterns

| anti-pattern | fix |
|---|---|
| rebuild a different artifact for production | build once, promote the artifact |
| manual steps in the release | automate; document exceptions as code |
| long-lived feature branches | trunk-based development + feature flags |
| tests that need a shared, persistent staging DB | ephemeral environments per PR |
| deploy Friday afternoon fear | small frequent releases, fast rollback, flags |
| pipeline credentials with admin rights | OIDC and least privilege |
| ignoring flaky tests | quarantine, fix, track flake rate |

code.source:
# GitHub Actions: lint/test in parallel, build once, scan, push by SHA, then deploy via OIDC (no long-lived keys)
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push: { branches: [main] }

permissions: { contents: read }          # least privilege by default

concurrency: { group: ci-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true }

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test }
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready" --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }      # dependency caching
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint && npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test
        env: { DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/postgres }

  build-and-push:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write, id-token: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with: { registry: ghcr.io, username: "${{ github.actor }}", password: "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" }
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}     # immutable tag = commit SHA
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
      - name: Scan image
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
        with: { image-ref: "ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}", severity: CRITICAL, exit-code: "1" }

# A deploy step as a script: promote the SAME image digest, wait for rollout, auto-rollback on failure
set -euo pipefail
IMAGE="ghcr.io/acme/api:${GIT_SHA}"
kubectl set image deployment/api api="$IMAGE"
if ! kubectl rollout status deployment/api --timeout=180s; then
  echo "rollout failed, rolling back" >&2
  kubectl rollout undo deployment/api
  exit 1
fi
# smoke test against the live service
curl -fsS https://api.example.com/healthz

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Whether you understand the **goals** of CI/CD (fast, safe, frequent change) and can design a pipeline and rollout strategy with sensible trade-offs.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Continuous integration, delivery and deployment?

**Model answer.** CI merges and tests every change frequently, producing a working build. Continuous delivery keeps the main branch always releasable with an automated path to production gated by a human decision. Continuous deployment removes that gate: every change passing the pipeline goes to production automatically. All depend on strong automated tests, small changes and fast rollback.

### 2. How would you design a CI/CD pipeline for a web service?

**Model answer.** On every PR: lint, type check, unit and integration tests (with containerised dependencies), dependency and secret scans, building the image. On merge to main: build once, tag with the commit SHA, push to a registry with an SBOM and signature, deploy to staging, run smoke and e2e tests, then promote the same artifact to production through a canary or rolling release with automated health checks and rollback. Pipeline-as-code, caching, parallel jobs and protected branches keep it fast and safe.

### 3. Blue-green versus canary deployments?

**Model answer.** Blue-green runs two full environments and switches all traffic at once, giving instant rollback but needing double capacity and database compatibility. Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version and increases it as metrics stay healthy, limiting blast radius and validating under real traffic but requiring good observability and traffic splitting. I'd use canary for risky changes to busy services and blue-green when I need atomic switches.

### 4. How do you handle database migrations in continuous deployment?

**Model answer.** With backward-compatible, multi-step migrations (expand, migrate, contract) since old and new application versions overlap during a rollout: add nullable columns or new tables first, deploy code that writes both and reads the new, backfill in batches, then remove the old structure in a later release. Migrations run as a separate pipeline step, are tested on production-like data, and are never destructive in the same release as the code that depends on them.

### 5. Why build the artifact once?

**Model answer.** What you tested must be exactly what you ship. Rebuilding per environment can pull different dependency versions or base images and change behaviour, invalidating the testing. An immutable artifact identified by a commit SHA or digest, promoted unchanged with environment-specific configuration injected at deploy time, makes releases reproducible and rollbacks trivial.

### 6. What is GitOps?

**Model answer.** Using Git as the single source of truth for the desired state of the infrastructure and applications; an in-cluster controller such as Argo CD or Flux continuously reconciles the cluster to match the repo. Changes go through pull requests, rollback is a revert, drift is corrected automatically, and CI doesn't need cluster credentials.

### 7. How do you secure the CI/CD pipeline?

**Model answer.** Least-privilege tokens, short-lived credentials via OIDC rather than stored cloud keys, secrets from a manager and never exposed to fork PRs, pinned third-party actions, ephemeral runners, protected branches and environment approvals. For the artifacts: dependency pinning and scanning, SBOMs, signed images and provenance, and verifying signatures at deploy.

## Rapid-fire

- **DORA metrics?** Deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore.
- **Best tag for deployed images?** Commit SHA or digest, not `latest`.
- **Cache what in CI?** Dependencies and build layers.
- **How to avoid long-lived cloud keys in CI?** OIDC federation.
- **Safest way to roll out risky code?** Canary + feature flag.

keyPoints: CI integrates and tests every change frequently; delivery keeps main releasable; deployment automates production release; DORA metrics measure the results.
Build once, tag by commit SHA, promote the same artifact; keep pipelines fast, reproducible and defined as code.
Use rolling, blue-green, canary and feature flags to limit blast radius; automate health checks and rollback; keep migrations backward compatible.
GitOps makes Git the source of truth for desired state with a pull-based reconciler.
Secure the pipeline: OIDC, least privilege, pinned actions, scanning, SBOM, signing and provenance.

options: What was tested is exactly what is deployed
check.q: Why promote the same built image through staging to production instead of rebuilding?
check.why: Rebuilding can change dependencies or base layers; promoting an immutable artifact preserves test validity.

options: A bad release affects only a small share of users and can be aborted early
It removes the need for rollbacks
check.q: What advantage does a canary release have over a big-bang deployment?
check.why: Exposing a small percentage first limits blast radius and lets metrics reveal problems before full rollout.

options: A long-lived admin key in the repo
A shared password in a wiki
check.q: How should a CI job authenticate to a cloud provider?
check.why: OIDC lets the job prove its identity and receive temporary scoped credentials, avoiding stored secrets.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code with Terraform
lessons.summary: Why manage infrastructure declaratively, Terraform's plan and apply cycle, state and remote backends, modules, environments, drift and safe change practices.

parts.label: IaC fundamentals
parts.body:
## Why infrastructure as code

Clicking through a cloud console doesn't scale: it is unrepeatable, undocumented, hard to review and impossible to recreate after a disaster. **Infrastructure as code (IaC)** describes servers, networks, databases and permissions in files that live in Git. Benefits: **repeatable** environments (dev, staging and prod from the same code), **review** through pull requests, **history and rollback**, **disaster recovery** (recreate everything), and **drift detection**.

**Declarative vs imperative:** declarative tools (Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi's model, Kubernetes manifests) state the **desired end state** and the tool computes the steps; imperative scripts say *how* (create this, then that). Declarative is idempotent by design: applying twice changes nothing the second time.

| tool | style | notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Terraform / OpenTofu** | declarative HCL | multi-cloud, huge provider ecosystem, state file |
| **Pulumi / CDK** | real languages (TypeScript, Python, Go) generating declarative plans | loops and abstractions, type checking |
| **CloudFormation / Bicep** | declarative, cloud-specific | deep native integration, no state file to manage |
| **Ansible** | procedural config management | configure machines already running |
| **Packer** | build images | bake machine/container images |

## Terraform's workflow

```
write .tf  →  terraform init  →  terraform plan  →  review  →  terraform apply
```

- `init` downloads providers and configures the backend.
- `plan` compares your code with the **state** and the real world and prints exactly what will be created (+), changed (~) or destroyed (-). **Always read the plan**, especially destroys and replacements (`-/+`).
- `apply` executes it. In teams, run plan automatically on every PR and apply only after merge, via CI (Atlantis, Terraform Cloud, GitHub Actions) with approvals.

## HCL building blocks

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6"
  required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" } }
  backend "s3" {                                  # remote state with locking
    bucket = "acme-tf-state"
    key    = "prod/network.tfstate"
    region = "eu-west-1"
    dynamodb_table = "tf-locks"
    encrypt = true
  }
}

variable "env" { type = string }
variable "instance_count" {
  type    = number
  default = 2
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
  bucket = "acme-${var.env}-assets"
  tags   = { Env = var.env }
}

data "aws_caller_identity" "current" {}      # data sources read things that already exist

output "bucket_arn" { value = aws_s3_bucket.assets.arn }
```

- **Resources** create things; **data sources** read existing ones; **variables** are inputs; **outputs** are results; **locals** are computed values.
- References (`aws_s3_bucket.assets.arn`) create a **dependency graph**; Terraform creates in the right order and in parallel where independent.
- `count` and `for_each` create multiple similar resources; prefer `for_each` with stable keys (removing an item from a `count` list shifts indices and can destroy resources).
- `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` protects critical resources; `create_before_destroy` for replacements without downtime.

parts.label: State, modules and safety
parts.body:
## State: Terraform's memory

Terraform stores a **state file** mapping each resource in your code to its real-world ID and attributes. It is how `plan` knows what exists. Consequences:

- **Never commit state to Git**: it can contain secrets in plain text.
- Use a **remote backend** (S3 + DynamoDB lock, GCS, Terraform Cloud) with **encryption and locking** so two applies can't run concurrently and corrupt state. Restrict who can read it.
- Split state into **small stacks** (network, data, apps; per environment) to limit blast radius and speed plans. Share values with `terraform_remote_state` or data sources.
- `terraform state list|show|mv|rm` and `terraform import` (adopt an existing resource) manage state; `moved` blocks refactor names without destroying.

## Drift

Someone changes a resource in the console, so reality no longer matches state and code. `terraform plan` reveals it (a diff you didn't make). Fix by re-applying the code (reverting the manual change) or updating the code to match. Prevent drift by restricting console write access and monitoring (`plan` on a schedule).

## Modules

A **module** is a reusable package of resources with inputs and outputs: a "vpc" module, a "service" module. They enforce standards (tagging, encryption, security groups) and cut duplication.

```hcl
module "web" {
  source        = "./modules/service"
  name          = "web"
  env           = var.env
  instance_type = "t3.small"
}
```

Keep modules small and opinionated, version them (Git tags or a registry), avoid deeply nested modules, and don't create a "god module" with 80 variables.

## Environments

Common approaches: a directory per environment (`envs/dev`, `envs/prod`) calling shared modules with different variables and separate state (clear, explicit, recommended); workspaces (same code, different state; easy to misuse). Promote infrastructure changes dev → staging → prod just like application code.

## Safe change practices

1. **Review plans** in the PR; use policy as code (OPA/Conftest, Sentinel, Checkov, tfsec) to block public buckets, unencrypted disks or open security groups.
2. **Least-privilege credentials** for the pipeline (OIDC, role per environment); humans don't apply to prod from laptops.
3. **Pin provider and module versions**; commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`.
4. Prefer **additive, small changes**; for dangerous ones (replacing a database), plan a migration.
5. **Secrets** never in `.tf` files or variables files in Git: reference a secret manager and mark sensitive outputs `sensitive = true` (still stored in state).
6. Tag everything (`Env`, `Owner`, `CostCentre`) for cost allocation.
7. Test: `terraform validate`, `fmt`, tflint, `terraform test`, Terratest for important modules, ephemeral preview environments.
8. Treat destroy as exceptional: `prevent_destroy`, deletion protection on databases, backups before changes.

## Immutable vs mutable infrastructure

Prefer **immutable**: never patch servers in place; build a new image/container and replace instances (autoscaling groups, Kubernetes). It eliminates configuration drift ("snowflake servers") and makes rollback a redeploy. Configuration management (Ansible) is for the cases where you must configure long-lived hosts.

code.source:
# Typical Terraform commands in CI (plan on PR, apply on merge)
terraform fmt -check -recursive
terraform init -input=false
terraform validate
terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan        # review this in the PR
terraform apply -input=false tfplan            # apply EXACTLY the reviewed plan (merge to main only)

# Adopt an existing resource into state, then refactor safely
terraform import aws_s3_bucket.assets acme-prod-assets
terraform state list

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Whether you understand IaC's **safety model**: state, plans, drift, blast radius and how teams change production infrastructure without incidents.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. What is Terraform state and why is it important?

**Model answer.** The state file maps resources declared in code to real infrastructure objects and stores their attributes, so Terraform can compute what to create, update or destroy. It must be stored remotely with encryption and locking, since it can contain secrets and concurrent applies could corrupt it. It is never committed to Git, and large estates are split into several small states to limit blast radius.

### 2. What happens if someone changes infrastructure manually in the console?

**Model answer.** That creates drift: reality differs from state and code. The next `terraform plan` shows the difference, and applying reverts the manual change unless the code is updated to match. To prevent it, restrict console write access, run scheduled drift-detecting plans, and make the pipeline the only path to production.

### 3. Declarative vs imperative provisioning?

**Model answer.** Declarative tools describe the desired end state and compute the actions, making runs idempotent, reviewable via plans and self-documenting. Imperative scripts list steps, which are flexible but must handle every starting state and tend to drift or break when re-run. I prefer declarative for infrastructure, and imperative only for glue.

### 4. How do you structure Terraform for multiple environments?

**Model answer.** Shared, versioned modules for standard building blocks, and a separate root configuration per environment with its own remote state and variables, so a mistake in dev can't touch prod and plans are small. Changes are promoted through environments by the pipeline. Workspaces can work for identical stacks but make it easy to apply to the wrong environment.

### 5. `count` or `for_each`?

**Model answer.** `for_each` over a map or set with stable keys is safer, because each instance is addressed by key. With `count` the instances are indexed by position, so removing an element from the middle of a list shifts the indexes and Terraform plans to destroy and recreate unrelated resources.

### 6. How do you make Terraform changes safe in production?

**Model answer.** Pull request review of the plan, policy-as-code checks, least-privilege pipeline credentials with approvals for production, version-pinned providers and modules, `prevent_destroy` and deletion protection on stateful resources, backups before risky changes, small incremental changes, and the habit of reading every destroy or replace in the plan.

### 7. What is immutable infrastructure?

**Model answer.** Servers are never modified after deployment; changes are made by building a new image or container and replacing the instances. It prevents configuration drift and snowflake servers, makes deployments reproducible and rollbacks a redeploy of the previous image.

## Rapid-fire

- **Where should state live?** Remote, encrypted, locked backend.
- **What does `plan` do?** Shows the diff between code, state and reality.
- **How to adopt an existing resource?** `terraform import`.
- **What's `OpenTofu`?** The open-source Terraform fork.
- **Secrets in state?** Possible; protect the state.

keyPoints: IaC makes infrastructure repeatable, reviewable and recoverable; declarative tools compute the steps from a desired end state.
Terraform workflow: init, plan (read it!), apply; run plan in PRs and apply from CI after merge.
State maps code to real resources: keep it remote, encrypted and locked, never in Git, and split it into small stacks.
Modules standardise patterns; use for_each over count, pin versions, and use one root configuration per environment.
Prevent drift and accidents with restricted console access, policy checks, prevent_destroy and least-privilege pipelines; prefer immutable infrastructure.

options: Removing an item does not shift the identity of the other resources
check.q: Why is for_each with stable keys safer than count for a list of resources?
check.why: count indexes by position, so removing a middle element renumbers later resources and may destroy and recreate them.

options: In Git next to the code
In a remote, encrypted backend with locking
check.q: Where should Terraform state be stored for a team?
check.why: State can hold secrets and must not be edited by two applies at once, so use a protected remote backend with locking.

options: terraform plan showing an unexpected diff
check.q: What reveals that someone changed a resource manually?
check.why: Plan compares real infrastructure with state and code, exposing drift as a diff.

lessons.title: Cloud fundamentals with AWS: compute, storage, networking, IAM, cost
lessons.summary: The shared responsibility model, regions and availability zones, core AWS services for compute, storage, databases and networking, IAM done right, high availability and cost control.

parts.label: Core ideas and compute
parts.body:
## Why the cloud

The cloud trades capital expense and lead time (buying servers) for **elastic, pay-per-use** infrastructure you can create in minutes via APIs. The cost of that flexibility is complexity and bills that grow quietly.

### Service models

- **IaaS** (EC2, virtual networks, block storage): you manage OS and up.
- **PaaS** (Elastic Beanstalk, App Runner, Cloud Run, managed databases): you manage code and config.
- **FaaS / serverless** (Lambda): you manage functions; scaling and servers are invisible.
- **SaaS**: you use the finished product.

### Shared responsibility

The provider secures **the cloud** (data centres, hardware, hypervisors, managed-service internals). You secure **what you put in the cloud**: IAM, network rules, OS patches on VMs, application code, data encryption, backups. Most cloud breaches are customer misconfigurations (public buckets, over-broad IAM, exposed keys), not provider failures.

### Geography and availability

- **Region**: a geographic area (eu-west-1) made of several isolated **Availability Zones (AZs)**: separate data centres with independent power and networking, connected with low-latency links.
- **Design for failure**: deploy across at least **2 to 3 AZs**; a single AZ is a single point of failure. Multi-region is for disaster recovery and global latency, at a much higher cost and complexity (data replication, consistency).
- **RTO/RPO**: recovery time objective (how long you can be down) and recovery point objective (how much data you can lose) drive the architecture: backup/restore (cheapest, slowest), pilot light, warm standby, active-active (fastest, most expensive).

## Compute options

| service | what | choose when |
|---|---|---|
| **EC2** | virtual machines (instance types by CPU/memory/GPU; spot, on-demand, reserved/savings plans) | full control, lift-and-shift, special hardware |
| **Auto Scaling Group + ALB** | a fleet that grows/shrinks behind a load balancer | stateless services on VMs |
| **ECS / EKS (+ Fargate)** | container orchestration (ECS simpler, EKS = Kubernetes; Fargate hides servers) | containerised workloads |
| **Lambda** | event-driven functions billed per request and millisecond; scales to zero | spiky, event-driven, glue code; watch cold starts, 15-minute limit, concurrency limits |
| **App Runner / Elastic Beanstalk** | managed web app platforms | small teams wanting simplicity |

Cost levers: right-size instances, use **Savings Plans/Reserved** for steady load (up to ~70 percent off), **Spot** for fault-tolerant work (up to ~90 percent off), scale to zero when idle, and Graviton (ARM) for better price-performance.

parts.label: Storage, data and networking
parts.body:
## Storage

- **S3** (object storage): virtually unlimited, 11 nines of durability, flat key namespace, eventually consistent semantics now strong read-after-write. Storage classes (Standard, Infrequent Access, Glacier) and lifecycle rules cut cost. Block public access by default, enable versioning and encryption, use presigned URLs for temporary access, and front it with CloudFront.
- **EBS** (block volumes for one EC2 instance), **EFS** (shared NFS file system), **FSx**.
- Choose by access pattern: objects (S3), a disk for one VM (EBS), shared POSIX files (EFS).

## Databases

| service | type | notes |
|---|---|---|
| **RDS / Aurora** | managed relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL) | backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover, read replicas; Aurora scales storage and replicas |
| **DynamoDB** | key-value / document NoSQL | single-digit-ms at any scale, partition-key design is everything, on-demand or provisioned capacity |
| **ElastiCache** | Redis/Memcached | caching, sessions, rate limits |
| **Redshift / Athena** | analytics warehouse / query S3 with SQL | OLAP |
| **OpenSearch** | search and log analytics | |
| **SQS / SNS / EventBridge / Kinesis** | queues, pub/sub, event bus, streams | decoupling and async |

Rule: use managed services for undifferentiated heavy lifting (backups, failover, patching) unless you have a reason to run your own.

## Networking: the VPC

A **VPC** is your private network in a region, divided into **subnets** per AZ.

- **Public subnet**: has a route to an **Internet Gateway**; hosts load balancers, bastions or NAT gateways.
- **Private subnet**: no direct inbound internet route; hosts application servers and databases. Outbound traffic goes through a **NAT Gateway** (costly: priced per hour plus per GB) or **VPC endpoints** (private access to S3/DynamoDB and other services without traversing the internet).
- **Security groups**: stateful, per-resource firewalls (allow rules only, reference other security groups: "the app tier may reach the DB on 5432"). **NACLs**: stateless subnet-level rules, rarely needed.
- **Route tables**, **VPC peering / Transit Gateway** (connect VPCs), **VPN / Direct Connect** (on-prem), **Route 53** (DNS, health checks, latency/geo routing), **CloudFront** (CDN), **ALB/NLB** (load balancing), **WAF/Shield** (protection).

Typical three-tier layout: ALB in public subnets → app servers/containers in private subnets across AZs → database in isolated private subnets; no database is ever publicly reachable.

parts.label: IAM, security and cost
parts.body:
## IAM: who can do what

**IAM** controls authentication and authorisation for AWS APIs. Concepts: **users** (people, avoid for humans: use SSO/IAM Identity Center), **groups**, **roles** (assumed temporarily by services, instances, Lambda functions and federated identities, with short-lived credentials), and **policies** (JSON documents of allow/deny statements on actions, resources and conditions).

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-prod-assets/*",
    "Condition": { "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "true" } }
  }]
}
```

Evaluation: **explicit deny wins**, then an explicit allow is required (default deny). Principles:

1. **Least privilege**: grant only the specific actions and resources needed; start narrow and widen using access analyzer findings.
2. **Roles, not keys**: give EC2/ECS/Lambda **instance/task roles** so applications get temporary credentials automatically; never embed access keys in code or images; CI uses OIDC.
3. **MFA** for humans, root account locked away with MFA and no keys.
4. Separate **accounts** per environment and team (AWS Organizations, Control Tower, service control policies) for blast-radius isolation and billing clarity.
5. Encrypt data **at rest** (KMS) and **in transit** (TLS); manage secrets in **Secrets Manager / Parameter Store**.
6. Turn on **CloudTrail** (audit log of API calls), **Config** (resource history and compliance), **GuardDuty** (threat detection) and alarms for root logins and policy changes.

## Well-Architected pillars (use as a checklist)

Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation, sustainability. Reliability in practice: multi-AZ, health checks and auto-healing, timeouts/retries, backups with tested restores, load testing, and game days.

## Cost control

- **Tag everything** and use Cost Explorer and budgets with alerts.
- Know the hidden costs: NAT Gateway data processing, cross-AZ and internet egress data transfer, idle load balancers, unattached volumes and old snapshots, over-provisioned databases, CloudWatch log volume.
- Right-size, schedule non-production environments off at night, use Spot and Savings Plans, S3 lifecycle policies, Graviton, serverless for spiky loads.
- Design with cost in mind: move data, not compute across AZs and regions; cache; compress; choose the right storage tier.

## Serverless trade-offs

Pros: no server management, automatic scaling, pay per use, built-in availability. Cons: cold starts, execution time and payload limits, vendor lock-in, harder local testing and debugging, per-request pricing that becomes expensive at sustained high volume (containers or VMs then win), and connection management to relational databases (use RDS Proxy).

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Cloud interviews test **architecture judgement**: availability, security by default, and cost awareness, using the provider's primitives sensibly.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Design a highly available web application on AWS.

**Model answer.** A VPC across three AZs: an Application Load Balancer in public subnets, application containers or instances in private subnets in an Auto Scaling Group or ECS service spread across AZs, a Multi-AZ managed database (RDS or Aurora) in isolated subnets, ElastiCache for caching, S3 and CloudFront for static assets, Route 53 with health checks for DNS. Security groups restrict each tier to the one above it; instances use IAM roles; secrets sit in Secrets Manager; logs and metrics go to CloudWatch with alarms. The stack is defined in Terraform and deployed through CI/CD. I'd add backups with tested restores and, if the RTO/RPO demands, a second region.

### 2. Security group versus network ACL?

**Model answer.** Security groups are stateful, attached to resources (network interfaces), support only allow rules and can reference other security groups, so return traffic is automatically allowed. NACLs are stateless, apply at the subnet level, have ordered allow and deny rules, and require explicit rules for return traffic. In practice security groups do most of the work and NACLs are coarse extra guardrails.

### 3. What is an IAM role and why prefer it to access keys?

**Model answer.** A role is an identity with permissions that a trusted entity assumes to receive short-lived, automatically rotated credentials. EC2, ECS and Lambda attach roles so no secrets live in code or config; long-lived access keys can leak and are hard to rotate and audit. People use SSO into roles, and CI uses OIDC to assume a role.

### 4. S3 versus EBS versus EFS?

**Model answer.** S3 is object storage accessed over HTTP, highly durable and cheap, for assets, backups and data lakes. EBS is a block device attached to a single EC2 instance (in one AZ) for boot volumes and databases. EFS is a managed NFS file system shared by many instances for POSIX file semantics. I choose by access pattern: objects, a disk, or shared files.

### 5. When would you use Lambda and when containers or EC2?

**Model answer.** Lambda for event-driven, spiky or low-volume work where scale-to-zero and zero ops matter: webhooks, file processing, scheduled jobs, glue. Containers or instances for steady high-throughput services, long-running tasks, special runtime needs, or when per-request pricing and cold starts hurt. I consider limits (timeout, payload), connection handling to databases, and total cost at expected volume.

### 6. How do you control and reduce cloud costs?

**Model answer.** Visibility first: tags, budgets, alerts and Cost Explorer. Then eliminate waste (idle resources, unattached volumes, oversized instances, forgotten environments), commit to Savings Plans for steady usage, use Spot for fault-tolerant work, S3 lifecycle tiers, VPC endpoints to avoid NAT data costs, caching and compression to cut egress, and schedule non-production environments. Cost is a design constraint, reviewed regularly.

### 7. RPO and RTO: how do they influence the design?

**Model answer.** RPO is the amount of data you can afford to lose and RTO how long you can be down. Tight RPO needs continuous replication (Multi-AZ, cross-region replicas), and tight RTO needs standby capacity and automated failover (warm standby or active-active); relaxed values allow cheaper backup-and-restore. I match the tier to the business impact and rehearse recovery.

## Rapid-fire

- **How many AZs for production?** At least two, preferably three.
- **Private subnet reaches the internet via?** NAT Gateway (or VPC endpoints for AWS services).
- **IAM evaluation default?** Deny; explicit deny overrides allow.
- **Which logs API activity?** CloudTrail.
- **Where store secrets?** Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.

keyPoints: Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud; you secure IAM, networks, data and applications.
Design for failure with multiple AZs; choose backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby or active-active from RTO and RPO.
Put load balancers in public subnets and apps and databases in private subnets; security groups reference each other; never expose databases publicly.
Use IAM roles with least-privilege policies instead of long-lived keys; enable MFA, CloudTrail and encryption with KMS.
Control cost with tags, budgets, right-sizing, Savings Plans, Spot, lifecycle rules and awareness of NAT and data-transfer charges.
